source_title: China Evergrande 2021 debt/liquidity crisis (named journalism: CNBC, Reuters, World Economic Forum summary)
publisher_issuer: Named journalism (CNBC, Reuters via Investing.com, World Economic Forum) reporting on Evergrande filings and bond payments
company_context: China Evergrande Group was one of China's largest property developers and, by 2021, the world's most indebted real-estate company. A liquidity crisis in 2021 raised fears of default with potential contagion across China's property sector and beyond.
business_type: Property developer (residential real estate; diversified conglomerate)
geography: China (Hong Kong-listed; offshore USD bondholders globally)
macro_context: China's 'three red lines' deleveraging policy tightened developer access to financing; the property sector accounted for roughly a quarter of China's economy, and a large share of Evergrande's obligations were pre-payments from homebuyers on undelivered units, creating acute social and systemic risk.
evidence_summary: By September 2021 Evergrande had more than $300 billion in liabilities and was warning investors it could default. Ratings agencies signalled imminent failure (Fitch said default 'appears probable'; Moody's said Evergrande was 'out of cash and time'). An estimated two-thirds of obligations were to homebuyers who had pre-paid for close to 1.4 million residential properties that remained undeveloped. In late September 2021 Evergrande sent $83.5 million to a Citibank trustee account to cover interest on a US-dollar bond, temporarily averting an immediate default, but the crisis reverberated across the ~$5 trillion Chinese property sector. (The company was ultimately ordered into liquidation by a Hong Kong court in January 2024 in a later development.)
owner_decision_context: Management had pursued debt-fuelled expansion and diversification, then faced a binary liquidity squeeze under tightened financing rules: whether to prioritise offshore bond coupons, supplier/wealth-product obligations, or completing pre-sold homes, with insufficient cash to meet all.
action_taken: Evergrande prioritised partial payments (e.g., the $83.5m coupon transfer in September 2021) and asset disposals to stave off formal default while negotiating with creditors; it pursued an extended offshore-debt restructuring over subsequent years.
outcome_evidence: Public default warnings, ratings agencies declaring default probable, >$300bn liabilities, and reliance on last-minute coupon transfers confirm a severe, systemically significant liquidity/solvency crisis (later culminating in a 2024 court-ordered liquidation).
source_limitations: WebFetch typically 403s here; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to CNBC, Reuters (via Investing.com) and the World Economic Forum. The '$300bn+ liabilities' and '1.4 million units' figures are widely reported from Evergrande disclosures/filings but not read by me in the primary filing. The 2024 liquidation order is a later event noted for context, not part of the 2021 source.
directly_stated: ~two-thirds of obligations owed to homebuyers on ~1.4 million undeveloped pre-sold properties
Fitch: default 'appears probable'; Moody's: 'out of cash and time'
$83.5m sent to a Citibank trustee for a USD bond coupon in September 2021, temporarily averting default
Chinese property sector ~$5 trillion, ~a quarter of the economy
inferred: Heavy reliance on homebuyer pre-payments as a financing source created a working-capital/solvency dependence that collapsed when new sales/financing slowed
The crisis was a leverage-driven solvency problem, not a temporary cash-timing issue
why_useful_for_opsiq: Non-US large-cap debt/solvency-and-liquidity crisis with systemic dimensions and an unusual financing model (homebuyer pre-payments as quasi-working-capital). Tests whether the engine identifies leverage-driven solvency pressure, distinguishes a near-term coupon payment from underlying insolvency, and routes ratings/default warnings into urgent re-evaluation.
